verdict: The taste is good and roughly 70% of the document is correct and well-argued — every number in the D1 limits table checks out verbatim against `src/content/docs/d1/platform/limits.mdx` (10 GB, 100 columns, 2 MB row, **100 bound params**, 1000 queries/invocation paid, 30 s, 50-byte GLOB, 50k databases, 1 TB, 30-day Time Travel); `PRAGMA foreign_keys=OFF` really is unavailable and `defer_foreign_keys` really is the documented mechanism; the Sessions API surface (`withSession('first-unconstrained'|'first-primary'|bookmark)`, Worker-binding-only, sequential consistency, no replica surcharge) is exactly right; the locale model (zero locale-named columns, partial-unique `x-default`, add-a-language-is-3-INSERTs) is the best part of the design and I could not break it; the R2 pointer pattern is the right call and the 2 MB row cap really does make inline manifests impossible; Stripe idempotency via PK + `stripe_updated_at` out-of-order guard is correct; and I confirmed by execution that `ON DELETE CASCADE` does fire the AFTER DELETE refcount triggers, as the comments claim. But it is not safe to build on as written. The document's central rhetorical move — "everything below was executed, not asserted" — is where it breaks: the headline claim **"zero table scans across all 20"** is false (I reproduced full `SCAN` on the two hottest public queries and on login), the headline **migration-safety rule #3 is a false mitigation that silently destroys data** (I reproduced it), and the **content-addressed GC will delete live R2 objects on the very first editor save of a large page** (I reproduced it). Separately, the ULID rationale rests on a billing model Cloudflare's pricing docs explicitly contradict, the "~60k tenants" runway measures only storage on a database containing no leads/audit/media/events, and the schema makes unmetered `claude-opus-5` generation free by CHECK constraint. Fix the eight fatal/major items below — most are 20–60 lines of SQL — and the bones are genuinely good.

fatal_flaws.claim: Migration strategy rule #3: 'Never rebuild a table that is the parent of an ON DELETE CASCADE FK without PRAGMA defer_foreign_keys=on first. D1 will cascade-delete children during the 12-step rebuild. PRAGMA foreign_keys=OFF is not available as an escape hatch.'
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: `defer_foreign_keys` defers *constraint violation checking* to end-of-transaction; it does not disable *foreign key actions*. I executed the 12-step rebuild on SQLite 3.45.1 with `PRAGMA defer_foreign_keys=ON` set first: `CREATE parent_new; INSERT SELECT; DROP TABLE parent; ALTER RENAME`. Both child rows were cascade-deleted, and `PRAGMA foreign_key_check` returned clean afterwards — silent, undetectable data loss. Since the doc correctly establishes that D1 forbids `PRAGMA foreign_keys=OFF`, the stated escape hatch does not exist and the rule as written is an instruction to destroy production data. In this schema `organisations` and `sites` are cascade parents of ~15 tables; one routine `sites` rebuild wipes every site_version, page, page_translation, media_asset, lead and job.
fatal_flaws.correction: Delete rule #3 and replace it with: a cascade-parent table can never be rebuilt in place on D1. Either (a) rebuild the *children* first — drop and recreate each child FK as NO ACTION, rebuild the parent, then restore — or (b) expand→migrate→contract only (rule #5 already covers every case you actually need, since ALTER TABLE ADD/DROP/RENAME COLUMN never triggers a rebuild), or (c) create a new table under a new name, dual-write, and retire the old one. Verify with `foreign_key_check` AND a row-count assertion on every child table in the same migration, because `foreign_key_check` passes after the damage.

fatal_flaws.claim: 'All 20 query patterns confirmed via EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN with zero table scans.' Q1 = 'SEARCH sites USING INDEX uq_sites_slug', Q2 = 'SEARCH custom_domains USING INDEX uq_domains_hostname'.
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: Every index on the soft-deleted tables is partial on `WHERE deleted_at IS NULL`, so it is usable only when the query text literally repeats that predicate — the *identical* failure mode the doc says it caught and fixed on `idx_jobs_queue`, left in place on the hottest queries in the product. Executed against the shipped schema: `SELECT id,published_version_id FROM sites WHERE slug='alpha'` → `SCAN sites`; `SELECT site_id FROM custom_domains WHERE hostname='x.com'` → `SCAN custom_domains`; `SELECT id FROM users WHERE email_normalized=?` → `SCAN users`; `SELECT id FROM media_assets WHERE site_id=? AND kind=?` → `SCAN media_assets`; leads inbox without the full `is_spam=0 AND archived_at IS NULL` predicate → `SCAN leads`. Q6 (`dashboard: my sites`) is worse: as written it plans `SCAN s` both before and after `ANALYZE`; it only becomes `SEARCH m USING COVERING INDEX idx_memberships_user` when `AND s.deleted_at IS NULL` is added. At 60k tenants a forgotten predicate turns one subdomain lookup into 60,000 `rows_read` on a single-threaded database. There is also no uniqueness backstop: `uq_sites_slug` and `uq_domains_hostname` are partial, so a soft-deleted row plus a re-created one means an unfiltered `WHERE slug=? LIMIT 1` can serve the *deleted* tenant's site, and a soft-deleted `custom_domains` row frees a hostname for another tenant to claim while the original `cf_custom_hostname_id` is still attached (note `uq_domains_cfid` is *not* deleted_at-scoped, so the scoping is inconsistent within one table) — that is the tenant-hijack the comment claims this index prevents.
fatal_flaws.correction: Either drop the soft-delete pattern for the identity-bearing tables (hard-delete into an archive table, so the unique indexes are total and every plan is seek-only), or keep it and enforce the predicate outside the query author's memory: expose reads through views (`CREATE VIEW live_sites AS SELECT * FROM sites WHERE deleted_at IS NULL`) or a query-builder that appends it, and add a CI check that runs `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` over every shipped statement and fails the build on any `SCAN`. Also add a *total* `UNIQUE(slug)` and `UNIQUE(hostname)` alongside the partial ones so a soft-deleted row still reserves its name.

fatal_flaws.claim: 'content_blobs refcounting -> drives the R2 garbage collector' and 'blobs can't be deleted while referenced' — verified.
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: There is no AFTER UPDATE trigger on `page_translations.content_sha256` or `blog_post_translations.body_sha256`. I executed it: a row pointing at blob A, updated to point at blob B, leaves A at refcount 1 and B at refcount 0. `idx_blobs_gc ON content_blobs(last_ref_at) WHERE refcount = 0` then hands the reaper a *live* blob to delete from R2 — the page renders blank for a paying tenant, permanently, with no error anywhere. This is not a theoretical path: it is exactly what the Phase-2 live editor does on every save of a page whose tree lives in R2 (which is all of them — 'page component trees always go to R2 regardless of size'), and what a `content_inline`→`content_sha256` promotion does when a page crosses 64 KB. The sealed-version triggers do not help, because drafts are freely updatable by design. The `ON DELETE RESTRICT` FK protects only the D1 row, never the R2 object. `last_ref_at` is likewise only ever written on INSERT, so even correctly-refcounted blobs carry a stale GC timestamp.
fatal_flaws.correction: Add `AFTER UPDATE OF content_sha256 ON page_translations WHEN NEW.content_sha256 IS NOT OLD.content_sha256` triggers (decrement OLD, increment NEW, bump `last_ref_at`) and the same for `body_sha256`; drop the `max(refcount-1,0)` clamp so drift aborts loudly instead of silently unlinking a live object. Then stop trusting the counter as the delete authority: add a `state` column to `content_blobs` ('live'|'tombstoned') and a two-phase reaper — mark tombstoned, wait past the grace window, re-verify refcount=0 under the same batch, then delete from R2 — and make the writer resurrect (`state='live'`) on dedupe hit rather than skipping the R2 PUT when a row already exists.

fatal_flaws.claim: 'Also trigger-enforced: a site's version pointer cannot reference another site's version. Cross-tenant pointer = data leak; cheap to make impossible.'
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: It is not impossible, and two adjacent columns have no guard at all. (1) `trg_sites_version_ownership` is `BEFORE UPDATE OF ...` only — I inserted a `sites` row whose `published_version_id` points at another org's `site_versions` row and it was accepted. The schema's own documented alternative insert path ('or one batch() with PRAGMA defer_foreign_keys = on') is precisely the path that bypasses the trigger. (2) `page_translations.site_version_id` is denormalised with no consistency guard: I inserted a translation of site 1's page stamped with site 2's `site_version_id`, and the public render query — which the comment says resolves '(version, locale, path) with ZERO joins' — then returns tenant 1's content under tenant 2's version. (3) `pages.site_id` is explicitly 'denormalised so org-scoped authorisation ... skip the version join', i.e. authorisation reads it, and I inserted a page belonging to site 2's version stamped `site_id = site 1`. So the one cross-tenant invariant that was made a trigger is incomplete, and the two columns that actually sit on the authorisation and render paths have none.
fatal_flaws.correction: Make the ownership trigger `BEFORE INSERT OR UPDATE`. Add BEFORE INSERT/UPDATE triggers asserting `page_translations.site_version_id = (SELECT site_version_id FROM pages WHERE id = NEW.page_id)` and `pages.site_id = (SELECT site_id FROM site_versions WHERE id = NEW.site_version_id)`, same for `blog_post_translations` and `blog_posts`. Better still, replace the denormalised columns with composite FKs — `UNIQUE(id, site_version_id)` on `pages` plus `FOREIGN KEY (page_id, site_version_id) REFERENCES pages(id, site_version_id)` — which the engine enforces on every write with no trigger to forget.

fatal_flaws.claim: The paywall: 'initial_site is free; every regenerate_* sets this to 1' and 'per-request/per-IP limiting uses the Workers Rate Limiting binding (wired in wrangler.toml). A write-per-request into a replicated SQLite database is an architecture bug, not a rate limiter.'
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: The CHECK gates only `regenerate*`. I executed inserts for all eight kinds with `requires_entitlement=0`: `initial_site`, `translate`, `blog_post`, `legal_docs`, `image_search` and `copy_rewrite` all succeed — six of eight AI job kinds, including the two largest token spends (6-locale translation and blog generation), run with no entitlement. And the stated mitigation cannot mitigate: per Cloudflare's own Rate Limiting docs, limits 'are local to the Cloudflare location that your Worker runs in' and the API is 'permissive, eventually consistent, and intentionally designed to not be used as an accurate accounting system' — so `RL_GENERATE` at 10/60s is 10 per *city*, ~300+ cities. The same doc also says 'it is not recommended to use IP addresses' as the key, which is what the design specifies. Cost per free generation, derived from the doc's own sizing model (12.5 MB inline per tenant / 144 page trees ≈ 87 KB of JSON per tree × 48 trees per version) is on the order of 1M output tokens; at claude-opus-5's $5/$25 per MTok that is roughly $5–$25 of Anthropic spend per unpaid signup, against €119,88/yr (~$128 gross, less VAT and Stripe fees) per paying customer. There is no budget gate anywhere in the write path — `usage_counters.limit_value` and `rate_limit_buckets` exist but nothing in the schema ties job dispatch to either.
fatal_flaws.correction: Move spend accounting to a Durable Object keyed by org (and by a signup-fingerprint pre-org), which is strongly consistent and is the correct Cloudflare primitive for money — the doc's own constraint list permits Durable Objects. Make `requires_entitlement` a function of cost, not of the word 'regenerate': gate every kind whose expected `cost_usd_micro` exceeds a threshold, and require a Stripe card (trial start) before the *first* generation, not before the second. Add a hard per-org and per-account daily USD ceiling checked in the same batch that flips a job to 'running', and cap `effort`/`max_tokens` for unpaid orgs (a schema CHECK can express `requires_entitlement=0 → effort IN ('low','medium')`).

fatal_flaws.claim: '~60k tenants per 10 GB database, measured' — and 'Beyond that, shard on org_id → database; the account allows 50,000 databases and 1 TB.'
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: Two problems. (a) The measurement is storage-only and was taken on a database containing *only* pages: I opened `sz.db` — 200 sites, 28,800 `page_translations`, and **zero rows** in `leads`, `audit_log`, `generation_job_events`, `media_assets`, `blog_posts`, `sessions`. Those are the tables that grow, and one of them is a bomb: `audit_log` 'doubles as the live-editor undo journal (before_json/after_json)' at up to 32 KB each, so ~160k slider drags fill the entire 10 GB database. That also violates the doc's own stated rule — 'D1 holds only what you filter, sort, join, or authorise on'; nobody filters on `before_json`. (b) The real ceiling is not storage. Cloudflare's D1 FAQ states 'Each individual D1 database is inherently single-threaded, and processes queries one at a time' and 'is backed by a single Durable Object'; replicas help reads only, 'All write queries are still forwarded to the primary'. Every lead capture, editor save, session touch and SSE job event from 60,000 tenants funnels through one single-threaded writer. Throughput bites years before 10 GB does. (c) The shard escape is a one-way door the schema itself blocks: `uq_sites_slug` is a global uniqueness constraint that cannot span databases; `users`↔`memberships`↔`organisations` is many-to-many across orgs; and `content_blobs` dedupes and refcounts *globally* — split it and one shard's GC deletes an R2 object another shard still points at.
fatal_flaws.correction: Re-measure with a realistic tenant (leads, audit, media, events, sessions) before quoting a runway. Move the undo journal off `audit_log` entirely — R2 blobs keyed by version, or a bounded ring of the last N edits per site with the payload in R2 — and give `audit_log` a `purge_after` column like `leads` has (it currently has only `idx_audit_purge` on `created_at`, which the doc describes as a 'retention column'). Then either commit to sharding now — slug allocation moves to a global registry (a Durable Object or a small control-plane D1), `content_blobs` becomes shard-local with no cross-shard dedupe, and identity lives in the control plane — or state explicitly that the product is capped at one database and size the write throughput accordingly.

fatal_flaws.claim: IDs: 'On D1 this is billed twice over: page reads count toward rows_read, and every dirtied page ships to read replicas.'
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: Both halves are contradicted by Cloudflare's pricing documentation. `src/content/partials/workers/d1-pricing.mdx` states: 'Rows read measure how many rows a query reads (scans), **regardless of the size of each row**' and, explicitly, 'Row size or the number of columns in a row does not impact how rows are counted. A row that is 1 KB and a row that is 100 KB both count as one row.' D1 bills rows, not pages — b-tree page locality has no billing consequence whatsoever. And note 10 of the same file: 'Read replication does not charge extra for read replicas. You incur the same usage billing based on rows_read and rows_written by your queries.' The b-tree-locality argument for time-ordered keys is still *technically* sound as a latency/cache argument; the economic justification stacked on top of it is invented. The companion argument ('ULID over UUIDv7 on key width: 26 chars vs 36') also compares against the worst UUIDv7 encoding — in a STRICT table a UUIDv7 is a 16-byte BLOB, narrower than a 26-char ULID, and the same document then stores sha256 as 64-char hex rather than a 32-byte BLOB, which by its own reasoning is the single most-duplicated value in the schema (`content_blobs` PK + `idx_blobs_gc` + `idx_blobs_kind` + `page_translations.content_sha256` + `idx_page_tr_blob`; `idx_blobs_kind` alone is 2.57 MB in the 200-tenant sizing DB, larger than several data tables and serving none of the 20 query patterns).
fatal_flaws.correction: Keep prefixed ULIDs — they are a fine choice — but justify them on debuggability and index-cache behaviour, not on a D1 billing model that does not exist. Store sha256 as BLOB(32) and drop `idx_blobs_kind` (no listed query uses it). Separately, `WITHOUT ROWID` is applied inconsistently: `sessions`, `memberships` etc. get it, but `organisations`, `sites`, `site_versions`, `pages`, `page_translations`, `media_assets`, `generation_jobs`, `leads`, `custom_domains` are rowid tables with TEXT PKs, so every point lookup is two b-tree descents (`Q12` plans as `SEARCH organisations USING INDEX sqlite_autoindex_organisations_1`, not 'USING PRIMARY KEY' as the doc reports) and each carries a full duplicate copy of the 30-char key (`sqlite_autoindex_page_translations_1` = 1.11 MB per 200 tenants).

fatal_flaws.claim: 'Immutability is a trigger, not a comment.' 'Sealed versions freeze content columns.' 'All three seal triggers abort.'
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: Sealing covers three of six mutation paths. I executed against a sealed, `status='published'` version: INSERT a new row into `pages` → allowed (there is a `trg_page_tr_sealed_insert` but no `trg_pages_sealed_insert`); DELETE a `page_translation` → allowed; DELETE a `page` → allowed; DELETE the sealed published `site_versions` row itself → allowed. That last one matters most: `sites.published_version_id` is `ON DELETE SET NULL`, so deleting a sealed published version silently unpublishes a live customer's site with no error and no audit trail, and simultaneously fires the refcount decrements that make its R2 blobs GC-eligible. 'Sealed' currently means 'certain UPDATEs are blocked', not immutable.
fatal_flaws.correction: Add `BEFORE INSERT ON pages` and `BEFORE DELETE ON pages` / `BEFORE DELETE ON page_translations` guards keyed on the parent's `sealed_at`, and a `BEFORE DELETE ON site_versions WHEN OLD.sealed_at IS NOT NULL AND OLD.status='published'` abort. Version retirement should be a status transition to 'archived' plus a separate, explicitly-unsealing purge job, not a DELETE.

fatal_flaws.claim: 'Public site render — read-only, tolerates lag → withSession("first-unconstrained"). Lowest global TTFB, which is what the 100/100 Lighthouse target actually needs.'
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: TTFB is not a scored Lighthouse metric. The performance score is a weighted composite of FCP, Speed Index, LCP, TBT and CLS; 'Reduce initial server response time' is an unweighted diagnostic. Lighthouse also runs from one fixed location under simulated throttling, so global replica placement is invisible to the score in a lab audit. More importantly, the render path itself is self-contradictory: `site_versions.bundle_sha256` is documented as 'built static bundle deployed to Pages', which would mean D1 is nowhere near the request path — but Q1/Q3 are described as per-request lookups, and the content lives in R2, so a page render is D1 (subdomain→version) → D1 (version,path→sha) → R2 GET (gzipped tree) → render, three serialized round trips. That is a materially worse LCP than a pre-rendered file on Pages, and it is the actual risk to the 100/100 target — not TTFB.
fatal_flaws.correction: Decide which it is and say so. If tenant sites are pre-built bundles on Pages (the right answer for 100/100 and for the single-threaded-D1 problem), then Q1/Q3 are not hot-path queries, the read-replication section is dead weight for the public site, and `page_translations` is a build-time source table — say that. If rendering is dynamic, put the rendered HTML in the Cache API / Cache Reserve keyed on `published_version_id` so a cache hit never touches D1 or R2, and justify it on LCP, not TTFB.

fatal_flaws.claim: 'Idempotency: retrying the same request never bills the customer twice' — `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX uq_jobs_idem ON generation_jobs(idempotency_key)`.
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: The index is globally unique across all tenants, not scoped to the org. I executed it: org2 inserting a job with a key org1 already used fails with `UNIQUE constraint failed`. Idempotency keys are conventionally client-supplied and frequently predictable (`gen-<slug>`, `gen-2026-01`, a UI-derived string). This gives any tenant a cross-tenant denial of service — burn a namespace of likely keys and other tenants' generations are rejected — plus an existence oracle for other tenants' keys.
fatal_flaws.correction: `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX uq_jobs_idem ON generation_jobs(org_id, idempotency_key)`. If the key is client-supplied, additionally hash it with the org id server-side so a tenant cannot even construct another tenant's key space.

fatal_flaws.claim: Validation CHECKs form a real type/format system: 'Passing a ver_… where a ste_… belongs now fails at write time'; `phone_e164 GLOB '+[0-9]*'`; `gbp_url GLOB 'https://*'`.
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: Each of these pins only a prefix and a length, with a trailing `*` that matches anything. Executed successfully against the shipped schema: `phone_e164 = '+1" onload=x'`, `whatsapp_e164 = '+31<script>'`, `gbp_url = 'https://" onmouseover=alert(1) x="'`, and `users.id = 'usr_0' + '!'*25` (30 chars, passes the 'CHECK-enforced type system'). These are not cosmetic: `whatsapp_e164` is by the blueprint's own spec interpolated into the sticky WhatsApp button's `href` (`wa.me/…`) and `phone_e164` into the LocalBusiness JSON-LD `telephone` field, on a page that also carries a cookie banner and a contact form — so a self-registered tenant controls a string that lands in an attribute and in a `<script type="application/ld+json">` block on their own public site (and, if a shared design/preview surface ever renders another tenant's values, beyond it). The `id` case also undermines the stated security rationale, since a CHECK constrains writes only and cannot stop a `WHERE id = <attacker string>` read.
fatal_flaws.correction: Anchor every pattern with a negated class: `phone_e164 NOT GLOB '*[^0-9+]*'` alongside the prefix test; `id NOT GLOB '*[^0-9A-HJKMNP-TV-Z_]*'` for Crockford base32; drop `gbp_url`'s GLOB in favour of length + server-side URL parsing. Then treat the database as the second line of defence, not the first — validate with Zod at the Worker boundary and HTML-escape/JSON-encode at render, because the doc's framing ('enforced by CHECK rather than convention') invites exactly the opposite.

fatal_flaws.claim: `reserved_slugs` protects system subdomains, and generated tenant sites live at `<slug>.mijnsaas.com`.
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: `reserved_slugs` has no FK, no trigger, and no reference from `sites` — I inserted a site with `slug='www'` and it was accepted. The table is decorative. Beyond that, hosting tenant sites on the same registrable domain as the app is a one-way door that no later migration fixes cheaply: `mijnsaas.com` is not on the Public Suffix List, so every tenant subdomain is same-site with the dashboard for `SameSite=Lax` purposes, any tenant can set cookies on `.mijnsaas.com` (cookie tossing against the session cookie), and `__Host-` prefixed cookies become unusable if the app is served from the apex. Slugs go into URLs, sitemaps and Google's index on day one, so moving them later costs every tenant their SEO.
fatal_flaws.correction: Enforce the reservation: `BEFORE INSERT OR UPDATE OF slug ON sites` aborting when `EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM reserved_slugs WHERE slug = NEW.slug)`, and extend the seed list with `_acme-challenge`, `autodiscover`, `mx`, `imap`, `pop`, `email`, `wpad`, and every label used by Cloudflare for SaaS. Then move tenant sites to a separate registrable domain (e.g. `mijnsaas.site`) and submit it to the Public Suffix List before launch — this is a Phase-1 decision, not a Phase-3 one.

fatal_flaws.claim: `media_assets.bytes INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (bytes > 0 AND bytes <= 524288000)` — 500 MB uploads, with `status` covering 'uploading'.
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: Per `workers/platform/limits.mdx`: 'Request body size limits depend on your Cloudflare account plan, not your Workers plan' — Free 100 MB, Pro 100 MB, Business 200 MB, Enterprise up to 5 GB; over-limit requests get a `413`. The hard constraint here is *Workers Paid*, which buys nothing on this axis, so a hero video anywhere above 100 MB cannot reach R2 through the Worker at all. The schema encodes a ceiling the platform will not honour, and there is no upload-session state (multipart `upload_id`, part list, presigned-URL expiry) to support the only mechanism that would work.
fatal_flaws.correction: Lower the CHECK to the real body limit for your zone plan, and for anything larger use R2 multipart with presigned URLs so bytes never traverse the Worker. That needs schema: an `upload_sessions` table (`media_id`, `r2_multipart_upload_id`, `parts_json`, `expires_at`, `state`), plus a reaper for abandoned multipart uploads — R2 bills for unaborted multipart parts indefinitely, which is a silent recurring cost on a product whose onboarding invites video uploads.

fatal_flaws.claim: GDPR handling: `ip_hash TEXT, -- sha256(ip || daily_salt) - not reversible, not personal data`, with `purge_after` and a purge cron.
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: A salted hash of an IP is pseudonymised personal data under GDPR, not anonymous — the controller necessarily holds the salt, and the IPv4 space is exhaustively enumerable in seconds, so re-identification is 'reasonably likely' in the Recital 26 sense. Writing 'not personal data' into the schema is a compliance assertion a Dutch/German DPA would reject, and this product's entire target market is EU small businesses acting as controllers for their own visitors. Operationally, the erasure path is also missing: `SELECT id FROM leads WHERE email=?` plans as `SCAN leads` (no index on `leads.email`), so a DSAR or right-to-erasure request is a full scan of the largest table, and `audit_log.before_json`/`after_json` can contain lead PII with no `purge_after` column and no erasure path at all.
fatal_flaws.correction: Delete the 'not personal data' comment and treat `ip_hash` as pseudonymous personal data in the ROPA and the generated privacy policy. Add an index supporting erasure-by-subject (`idx_leads_email ON leads(email) WHERE email IS NOT NULL`, plus phone), give `audit_log` a real `purge_after` column, and add a documented erasure procedure that covers `leads`, `audit_log`, and the R2 objects referenced from both. Rotate the daily salt and delete old salts, or drop `ip_hash` entirely and rely on Turnstile for anti-spam.

fatal_flaws.claim: Verification defect #1: '`idx_jobs_queue` degraded to a full table SCAN … Fixed to a plain composite — `status` is the leading column, so it seeks the live range anyway and ORDER BY queued_at needs no sort.'
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: The diagnosis is right and the fix is wrong. I reproduced both halves: with the partial index, `WHERE status='queued'` does `SCAN` (SQLite's prover cannot derive the implication) — but `WHERE status IN ('queued','running','streaming') ORDER BY queued_at`, which is how a multi-status queue drain is actually written, **does** use the partial index (`SEARCH j USING INDEX ix_partial`). So the partial index was usable; only the query text was wrong. Meanwhile the shipped non-partial `idx_jobs_queue(status, queued_at)` reintroduces a sort on exactly that drain: `WHERE status IN ('queued','running','streaming') ORDER BY queued_at LIMIT 5` plans as `SEARCH … USING INDEX idx_jobs_queue` **+ `USE TEMP B-TREE FOR ORDER BY`**, contradicting 'ORDER BY queued_at needs no sort'. And because it is no longer partial, the index grows forever with terminal jobs — at 10k tenants the live queue is a few dozen rows inside an index of millions of `succeeded` entries, on the table with the highest write churn in the schema (four status transitions per job, each rewriting the index entry).
fatal_flaws.correction: Restore the partial index and fix the query to carry the predicate verbatim (`WHERE status IN ('queued','running','streaming') AND …`), or — better for a lease-based queue — make it a sentinel: a nullable `queue_ready_at` set on enqueue and NULLed on terminal transition, with `CREATE INDEX idx_jobs_queue ON generation_jobs(queue_ready_at) WHERE queue_ready_at IS NOT NULL`, which is small, sorted, and immune to predicate-matching. Separately, polling a single-threaded D1 from a cron gives a minimum ~60 s enqueue-to-start latency on a product whose entire UX is a live 'magic popup' progress bar — Cloudflare Queues is on the permitted list and is not used.

fatal_flaws.claim: Anthropic call parameters 'recorded verbatim for reproducibility': `thinking_type` and `effort` as independent columns; `thinking_tokens INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0`.
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: On `claude-opus-5`, `thinking: {type: "disabled"}` is accepted only at effort `high` or below and returns a 400 at `xhigh`/`max`. The schema allows and will happily record `thinking_type='disabled'` with `effort='xhigh'` — a combination the API rejects — which is precisely the class of invariant this document argues belongs in a CHECK rather than a comment, and it is the one Anthropic invariant that is cheaply expressible. Separately, the Messages API `usage` object has no thinking-token field: thinking is billed inside `output_tokens`. `thinking_tokens NOT NULL DEFAULT 0` will always be 0, and any `cost_usd_micro` formula that adds it to `output_tokens` double-counts. Minor by comparison, but this is the one section the document claims is 'recorded verbatim'.
fatal_flaws.correction: Add `CHECK (thinking_type <> 'disabled' OR effort IN ('low','medium','high'))`. Drop `thinking_tokens` or rename it to make clear it is a derived estimate, not a reported usage field. Also note `cache_prefix_sha256` models one cache breakpoint while the API allows four — if the industry prompt fragment and the base system prompt are separate breakpoints, one hash cannot attribute hit rate. And the flagged risk in 'One thing I'd flag' is a non-issue: D1 documents generated columns explicitly (`d1/reference/generated-columns`), including VIRTUAL as the default and adding them via ALTER TABLE, so `duration_ms` will apply cleanly.

missing: A written consistency contract for the SSE progress feed. Job events are polled from D1, and the dashboard is documented as using bookmarks for read-your-writes — but the SSE poller is a different request path, and `first-unconstrained` on a replica will show a stuck progress bar during the exact minutes the user is staring at it. Nothing in the design says which constraint the SSE path uses.

Any write-throughput budget. The document reasons about storage, index coverage and rows_read, but never estimates writes/second against Cloudflare's stated 'each individual D1 database is inherently single-threaded, and processes queries one at a time'. `generation_job_events` alone (3 indexes + a `sqlite_sequence` row per AUTOINCREMENT insert) is a high-frequency write stream during every generation, on the same single writer that serves lead capture and editor saves.

`content_inline` is dead code on `page_translations`. The rule 'page component trees always go to R2 regardless of size' means the inline branch of the XOR is never taken — confirmed in the author's own sizing database: 28,800 rows, 28,800 with `content_sha256`, 0 with `content_inline`. The elaborately-documented 64 KB threshold and the 'XOR fires both ways' verification apply to a column nothing writes.

A row for the bare root path. Every `page_translations.path` includes a locale segment (`/en/`, `/nl/`), so `https://<slug>.mijnsaas.com/` matches no row. The x-default redirect/rewrite is unmodelled, and it is the single most-requested URL on every tenant site.

Stripe/EU tax reality. `subscriptions.currency` defaults to 'eur' and `invoices` carries `tax_cents`, but there is no VAT rate, no reverse-charge flag, no OSS reporting fields, and no `stripe_tax_calculation_id` — for a B2C/B2B EU SaaS at a single €9,99 price point across 6+ countries, VAT is a Phase-1 schema concern, not a Phase-3 one.

`uq_stripe_customers_org` makes the org↔Stripe-customer mapping permanently one-to-one, and both `stripe_customers.org_id` and `subscriptions.org_id` are ON DELETE RESTRICT. Recreating a Stripe customer (entity change, country move, Stripe-side deletion) is not expressible without deleting a row the RESTRICT blocks.

The paywall's denormalised `organisations.entitlement` has no trigger, no view, and no reconciliation job keeping it consistent with `subscriptions.status` — the one business-critical invariant in the schema is enforced by the comment 'written by the Stripe webhook in the same batch()', in a document whose thesis is that comments are not enforcement. Stripe retries webhooks for up to three days; the `idx_orgs_entitlement_expiry` cron partially covers expiry but nothing covers divergence.

No ANALYZE / `sqlite_stat1` strategy. Several plans in this schema flip depending on whether statistics exist (I reproduced Q6 changing after ANALYZE), and D1 does not run ANALYZE for you. If the shipped plans were verified on an empty database, they are not the plans production will use.

Verification of the cited `wrangler` trigger-splitter bug (workers-sdk#10998). Isolating triggers in their own migration is good practice regardless, but I could not confirm the issue exists from this environment, and the specific claim that lowercase `begin` is the trigger of the bug is load-bearing enough in the doc's rationale that it should be linked to something reproducible.

A migration smoke-test harness. Given that migration rule #3 as written destroys data and `foreign_key_check` passes afterwards, every migration needs a CI gate that snapshots per-table row counts before and after and fails on any unexplained drop — plus the Time Travel bookmark the doc already recommends, actually wired into the pipeline rather than described.
